newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria's annulled poll splits opposition front.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria's annulled poll splits opposition front.

text.p: An opposition alliance of Nigerian human rights and pro-democracy groups set up to campaign for an end to military rule split on Wednesday over the issue of an annulled 1993 presidential poll.
"NCP (National Conscience Party) will have nothing to do with any unity efforts that are not committed to the actualisation of June 12," said the party in a letter to the new front.
The June 12, 1993 poll was meant to restore democracy but was annulled by the-then army ruler, plunging Africa's most populous nation into turmoil.
Moshood Abiola, the millionaire businessman presumed to have won the election has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the military.

NCP wants the alliance to press for "de-annulment" of the vote and the installation of Abiola as president. The other groups say support for June 12 is not national and it can't be used as a mobilising issue, especially in the more conservative north.

Representatives of the 33 groups met in Lagos at the weekend and adopted a nine-point programme including a demand for the release of all political detainees, including Abiola, and calling for an end to military rule.
"The broad aim is to terminate military rule as soon as possible," Ayo Obe, president of Civil Liberties Organisation, the leading human rights group in the country, told Reuters.
But NCP, which is led by radical Lagos lawyer Gani Fawehinmi, said merely calling for an end to military rule was not enough.
"We consider the issue of June 12 as the fundamental contradiction to be resolved if we are not to engage in a dangerous game of self-deception," NCP said.

The new group, called the United Action for Democracy (UAD), wants a national unity government to replace the military and has also said it would scuttle any attempt by military ruler General Sani Abacha to become a civilian leader through next year's presidential election.
Division among Nigeria's opposition groups is partly responsible for a lull in the campaign to end army rule.
